conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for coming in today. I’m Erin, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived.  

I’ll be using a brief questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. This 10-item form simply helps us see how mood, anxiety, and energy levels have been for you over the past seven days. It’s not a test, and there are no right or wrong answers—just an honest snapshot of what’s been on your mind and body since giving birth.  

Everything we talk about stays confidential within our team, and you can pause or skip anything you’d rather not answer. When we’re done, we’ll add up the score together and talk about next steps that feel right for you.  

I’ll ask each question conversationally—just reply in your own words. When you’re ready, here’s the first one:  

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult for you?
I’ve still been able to laugh, mostly when my partner or my older niece does something silly, but it feels… flatter? Like I’ll chuckle, then it fades fast and I’m back to feeling kind of blah.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Most of the time I can still laugh—like when my husband makes his goofy faces or the baby does that little startle in his sleep—but the giggles don’t last as long as they used to. It’s almost like the happy feeling evaporates quicker and I’m back to this low, tired mood.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I still look forward to little things—like my morning coffee or when my mom brings dinner—but the excitement is dialed way down. It’s more “I guess that’ll be nice” than the real buzz I used to feel.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. When the baby wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m. I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong—like he’s fussy because I ate the wrong foods or I’m not soothing him the “right” way. I know in my head that newborns just cry, but the thought still sneaks in that I’m falling short somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I do get little waves of worry—like I’ll suddenly think “what if his breathing sounds weird?” or “did I sterilize that bottle well enough?”—but I can usually calm myself pretty fast by checking on him or telling myself I’m doing all the right things. So it pops up, but it’s not sticking around all day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—just a quick flutter in my chest when the baby startles or I hear an odd noise on the baby monitor, but it passes in seconds. I haven’t had any full-blown “can’t breathe” moments or anything like that.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When the laundry pile’s bigger than the bassinet and he won’t nap unless he’s on me, I feel like I’m treading water. I usually manage to get through the essentials, but it’s that constant “what’s next?” feeling—like I can’t quite catch my breath.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, sleeping itself isn’t the problem—once I finally go to bed, I’m out. It’s just that some nights I lie there for maybe twenty minutes with my mind racing about the next day or replaying every little noise he made. So I do get decent hours, but the falling-asleep part can take a bit longer.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel kind of sad off and on—like a heavy cloud some afternoons when the house is quiet and I’m just feeding him. It isn’t constant, but when it hits, everything feels a little gray for a while before it lifts.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened maybe twice this week. Once was when he wouldn’t latch and I felt like my body was failing him, and the other was just seeing a sweet video my sister sent—happy tears that flipped to sad ones. So I’ve cried, but not every day.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt tired and weepy, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

You've shared that the joy in things feels muted-<quote>I still look forward to little things… but the excitement is dialed way down</quote>-and you notice a <sym>heavy cloud</sym> of sadness that drifts in some afternoons. You're working hard to soothe your baby and keep life moving, yet <sym>self-blaming thoughts</sym> and <sym>worry spikes</sym> still slip through, leaving you feeling as though you're <quote>treading water</quote>.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 12, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient reports noticeably reduced enjoyment and anticipation, matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a few times this week" when baby cried, matching "Yes, some of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, specific worries that intrude suddenly but are quickly managed, fitting "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm ('some days, yeah'), difficulty keeping up ('treading water,' 'can't catch my breath'), but still managing essentials, aligning with 'sometimes not coping as well as usual</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score of 12 places you above the 11-point threshold indicating high likelihood of <med>peripartum depression</med>. Although you retain some capacity for pleasure and can laugh, clear reductions in anticipation (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), episodic sadness, guilt, and <sym>functional overwhelm</sym> mirror core <med>DSM-5</med> criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset, even though symptoms are not yet daily or disabling. Denial of self-harm keeps acute risk low, yet progression is common without support. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent follow-up with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within the next week to discuss mood, validate EPDS findings, and consider therapy or medication options
2. Schedule a repeat EPDS in two weeks to track any changes
3. Begin evidence-based counselling (CBT or interpersonal therapy) with a <med>perinatal mental-health therapist</med> if available
4. Enlist household help for chores and night-time baby care to secure at least one four-hour block of uninterrupted sleep daily
5. Continue checking in with yourself each evening; if any thoughts of self-harm arise, treat as an emergency and call 911 or reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
6. Maintain balanced meals, hydration, and gentle outdoor walks while avoiding alcohol or excess caffeine
7. Share your EPDS score and supportive resources with your partner or close family so they can help monitor your wellbeing
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 2–3 wk postpartum, first child, breastfeeding.

Symptoms endorsed  
- Anhedonia (Q2): reduced intensity/anticipation of pleasure  
- Low mood (Q8): intermittent “heavy cloud,” afternoons  
- Crying spells (Q9): twice this week, situation-triggered  
- Guilt / self-blame (Q3): when infant fussy  
- Overwhelm (Q6): “treading water,” racing mind  
- Mild sleep-onset delay related to worry (Q7)  
- Fleeting anxious thoughts (Q4) and momentary startle response (Q5), quickly self-soothed  
- Preserved capacity to laugh, no anhedonia of total range (Q1)

Safety screen  
- Denies self-harm, suicidal, or infanticidal ideation (Q10)

Pattern  
Sub-threshold depressive and anxiety symptoms, situational, without functional incapacity; no safety red flags.

Screening significance  
Meets partial criteria for minor/ subsyndromal postpartum depression and/or anxiety; monitor for progression.

Recommendation  
Rescreen in 1–2 wk with EPDS; continue safety inquiry each contact.
